Question six. What is source freshness, and how is it different from a test? A test checks what the data says. Freshness checks the clock: how old the newest row is, read from a loaded-at column. This source warns after six hours and errors after twelve. Its newest row landed at one in the morning. Checked at nine, it's eight hours old: a warning. At two in the afternoon, thirteen: an error. And all four tests pass on it. The rows that are there are valid; they're just old. So dbt source freshness runs before the models build. It has two thresholds because a feed slipping later each day is the usual signal, and the warning catches the slip before the outage.

Question seven. How does CI for analytics typically work? On every pull request, continuous integration runs dbt build on the models that changed, and everything downstream of them. It finds the changes by comparing the project with production's manifest, its record of what's deployed. Change the customer staging model here, and three of the four models are built and tested. Orders staging is left alone. That's slim CI: fast feedback without rebuilding every model, and a failing test blocks the merge. Question eight. How do you respond to a failing test in CI versus in production? In CI, the merge is blocked: fix the model or the test before it ships. In production, go by severity. An error halts everything downstream and pages the owner, so the marts keep yesterday's rows instead of taking bad ones. A warning is triaged later. Either way, read the failing rows, decide whether the data or the assumption is wrong, and fix the cause. Never loosen the test just to make it pass.
